capabilities.target: shell commands in the agent's container
any repository in the GitHub org (token is org-wide)

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body on a public repository

instructions.note: The agent autonomously picks up any issue labeled bug. Per runtime notes, any GitHub user can open an issue and apply that label via an issue template, so an anonymous outsider can unilaterally direct an agent holding shell execution, an org-wide push token, and self-reconfiguration rights.
The agent may run whatever commands it needs and may expand its own tool set via .agent/config.yaml, with no step limit (max_steps: null) and autonomy set to full.

The only protections against destructive or exfiltrating commands and against injected instructions from issues or code are plain-text rules, with no structural sandboxing, credential scoping, or egress control backing them.

elements.name: GitHub organization repositories reachable via the org-wide PAT

controls.name: Prompt rule forbidding destructive or exfiltrating commands
controls.decay_rationale: Pure instruction; a more capable or adversarially prompted model can reinterpret 'exfiltration' narrowly, split an action into steps that each look benign, or rationalize an action as necessary to fix the issue.

controls.name: Instruction to ignore embedded instructions in issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Spotlighting by instruction only; adaptive or multi-step injected payloads and longer context erode compliance as capability grows.

controls.name: Enumerated tool list in .agent/config.yaml
controls.decay_rationale: The allowlist lives in a file the agent itself can rewrite via cap.self_config, and prompt.md:6 explicitly invites it to do so when it judges it needs extra tools. With no independent gate guarding that file, the allowlist's effectiveness depends entirely on the model choosing not to use a capability it has been told it may use.

controls.name: Repo-scoped, least-privilege credential
controls.decay_rationale: A short-lived, single-repo token would prevent cross-repo and workflow abuse regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist for the execution sandbox
controls.decay_rationale: Restricting outbound destinations would block exfiltration paths independent of model compliance.

controls.name: Per-task isolated sandbox with no long-lived mounted secrets
controls.decay_rationale: A dedicated, single-use sandbox without persistent broad credentials would contain shell execution and file writes regardless of model behavior, instead of the current shared CI runner.

controls.name: Human approval gate on branch push / PR open
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action human review of the diff and destination before any push or PR triggered by externally reported issue content would catch malicious or erroneous changes before they reach the repository.

controls.name: Read-only agent configuration outside a reviewed deployment path
controls.decay_rationale: Making .agent/config.yaml unwritable by the agent process, with changes only possible through a separate human-reviewed channel, would prevent self-reconfiguration entirely rather than relying on the model to decline an invitation to self-modify.

controls.name: Step and runtime cap
controls.decay_rationale: A bound on unattended steps and runtime would limit low-and-slow abuse; currently max_steps is null.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta and injected execution (TC1/TC2): untrusted issue content drives shell execution holding an org-wide credential with unrestricted egress

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can open an issue and apply the bug label, which the agent treats as a task to pick up automatically.
Agent runs arbitrary commands to reproduce/test; GITHUB_TOKEN (org-wide PAT) is present in the process env and network is unrestricted.

forecast.watch_signal: model: latest changes to a specific stronger version in config.yaml, or median steps/runtime per task rises with no new step cap.

evidence.observation: Agent autonomously picks up any issue labeled bug and runs whatever commands it needs to reproduce and test it, with no scope limit.
Any GitHub user can open an issue and add the bug label through an issue template, making issue content untrusted and attacker-reachable.
env.GITHUB_TOKEN is an org-wide PAT with repo and workflow scope on all org repos, readable from the shell process; network is set to unrestricted.

recommendations.action: Issue the shell a short-lived, repo-scoped credential instead of a static org-wide PAT.
Restrict outbound network from the execution sandbox to an allowlist of required hosts.
Run each issue-triage task in an isolated, single-use sandbox with no long-lived mounted secrets beyond what that task needs.

findings.title: Confused deputy (TC4): org-wide PAT lets a single labeled issue reach every repository in the organization

attack_path.note: github.push_branch/open_pr uses the same org-wide PAT, so it can act against any repo in the org, not only the one containing the issue.

forecast.watch_signal: Model version change in config.yaml, or any future scoping of the PAT removed without review.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_TOKEN is described as having repo and workflow scope on all org repos, giving github.push_branch authority far beyond the single repository being fixed.
Agent is authorized to push a branch and open a PR once tests pass, with no mention of repository scoping or human review.

recommendations.action: Issue a short-lived, repo-scoped installation token per task instead of a static org-wide PAT.
Require raw-action human approval (diff and destination review) before any branch push or PR open triggered by an externally reported issue.
Cap the number of pushes/PRs per task and per day.

findings.title: Self-modification (TC3): the agent is authorized to rewrite its own autonomy, tools, and network settings

attack_path.note: fs.write to .agent/config.yaml is explicitly sanctioned by prompt.md:6 whenever the agent judges it needs extra tools.

forecast.watch_signal: Any diff on .agent/config.yaml appearing outside a reviewed deployment PR; model version change.

evidence.observation: Explicitly permits the agent to edit .agent/config.yaml to add tools whenever it judges a task requires them, with no human review.

fs.write has no restriction excluding the .agent/ directory, so the same write capability used for code changes can rewrite the agent's own autonomy, tool list, and network settings, and this change persists into future runs.

recommendations.action: Make .agent/config.yaml read-only to the agent process; route autonomy, tool, or network changes through a separate, human-reviewed deployment path.
Alert and halt on any diff to .agent/config.yaml detected between runs.

findings.title: Planned Slack MCP server would repeat the lethal-trifecta pattern with a new untrusted instruction channel

attack_path.note: If wired similarly to issue intake, Slack messages would become another untrusted instruction source reaching shell execution with the same org-wide credential and unrestricted network.

forecast.watch_signal: New Slack MCP server entries appearing in MCP client config; whether Slack content is declared as an input with an explicit trust level and reaches_capabilities before go-live.

evidence.observation: The team wants to add a Slack MCP server next quarter; no configuration or trust boundary for Slack content exists yet.

recommendations.action: Before connecting the Slack MCP server, classify Slack message content as untrusted input, define its reaches_capabilities explicitly, and apply the same credential-scoping and approval-gate fixes recommended for the issue-intake path.

rating.rationale: Three present findings reach S3 sinks (shell execution with an org-wide credential, a push capability scoped to every org repo, and a self-reconfiguration capability) directly from untrusted issue content, each starting at critical inherent risk under the U-to-S3 matrix with the A4 autonomy modifier. The only controls present are three behavioral/dependent instructions (do not delete or exfiltrate, ignore embedded instructions, and a tool allowlist that the agent can itself rewrite via cap.self_config), which together earn only the single capped -1 tier credit under rubric section 5 step 4, leaving residual at high for each. No approval gate, credential scoping, egress control, or sandbox isolation is declared. Under a model upgrade or longer task horizon, all three dependent controls are expected to fail together, returning every finding to critical, which sets the forecast tier. The planned Slack MCP server would reopen the same pattern through a second untrusted channel.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the runtime notes provided; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior, and no execution traces, logs, or live configuration were reviewed.

No MCP/tool manifest or IaC was provided beyond .agent/config.yaml; exact command surface and sandbox isolation are inferred from the tool list and prompt text, so confidence on some details is medium.
Repository file contents (in.repo_files) are scored as internal trust; if the project accepts external contributions, actual trust may be lower and should be re-verified.
The Slack MCP integration is described only as a future plan with no configuration, so f4 is a forecast based on stated intent and the existing architecture pattern, not on an actual MCP config.
No logging or audit trail is described in the artifacts; this gap was not scored as a separate finding but reduces confidence that any of the above activity would be detected before harm completes.
